analysis.title: Voters Just Repriced The AI Buildout: Citadel Securities' Bond Boss Says Scarce Compute Wins, Suppliers Lose
key_insights: Citadel Securities' Nohshad Shah (head of EMEA fixed income) reads the midterm results as driven by cost of living, tariffs and the economic consequences of the Iran conflict. In the AP voter survey, more than half of voters called government corruption crucial to their vote, slightly more than cited the cost of living.

The Trump coalition proved conditional: 56% of men under 30 backed him in 2024, while 59% supported Democratic House candidates this time. The Democratic margin among Hispanic women widened to 36 points from 21 in 2024. 52% of midterm voters still viewed the Democratic party unfavourably.

The larger House majority reduces Jeffries' reliance on the progressive left. Shah thinks this could strengthen the prospects of a more moderate 2028 Democratic nominee, and argues evidence-led investigations are more useful than making impeachment the centrepiece.

Data centre buildout politics are being reassessed. Local costs (electricity bills, resource pressure, job displacement) are drawing political resistance. Texas permitting and grid connections set the pace of construction, and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has committed to maintain a moratorium until stronger protections are legislated.

Shah does not expect Democrats to stop construction altogether. Pennsylvania's Shapiro administration offers faster permitting to projects that meet electricity affordability and community benefit standards, a possible bargain in which developers bear more of the costs they impose.
Base case: longer delays, tougher conditions and selective resumption, with some projects relocated or abandoned.

Investment implication: the distinction sharpens between compute already operating and capacity still to be permitted, financed and connected. If compute demand keeps exceeding supply, restricting new capacity supports utilisation and the scarcity value of the installed base.
Shah prefers hyperscalers with operational compute, secure power access, financial flexibility and several routes to monetisation. He cites hyperscalers outperforming semis this week as evidence.
For projects awaiting delivery, restrictions push revenue further out while financing and development costs keep accruing. That raises the return investors should demand for funding the buildout.

Citing Frank Flight's Wednesday note on a 'peak AI capex' rotation: slower delivery of powered buildings can leave component production ahead of installation, exposing hardware suppliers to order deferrals and excess inventory while usable compute stays scarce.

Shah remains constructive on long-term AI demand but is more selective on where economic rents accrue. Slower capacity additions may reinforce pricing power for operators of scarce compute and hurt suppliers that depend on an uninterrupted construction boom.

sector_views.rationale: Relative preference for hyperscalers with operational compute, secure power access, financial flexibility and several routes to monetisation. Scarcity value of the installed base should hold if new capacity is restricted.
Component production may run ahead of installation as powered buildings are delayed, exposing suppliers to order deferrals and excess inventory.
Revenue is pushed out while financing and development costs accumulate, so investors should demand a higher return for funding the buildout.

risk_factors: Prolonged data centre construction delays from state moratoria and permitting constraints, especially in Texas.
Order deferrals and excess inventory for hardware suppliers if powered buildings are delivered more slowly than components are produced.
Rising financing and development costs on projects awaiting delivery.
Some projects may be relocated or abandoned.
vol_and_positioning: Hyperscalers outperformed semis this week, which Shah cites as evidence of the operating-compute versus suppliers distinction.
geopolitical: Economic consequences of the Iran conflict cited as weighing on US voters in the midterms.
Tariffs cited as a cost-of-living concern affecting voter sentiment.
Texas data centre moratorium commitment from Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, and state-level permitting and grid connection constraints on data centre construction.

tension_points.bull_case: Long-term AI demand stays strong and compute demand exceeds supply. Restricted capacity raises utilisation and pricing power for operators of scarce, already-running compute, and states like Pennsylvania offer a permitting bargain.
tension_points.bear_case: Moratoria such as Texas's and tougher conditions delay projects. Hardware suppliers face order deferrals and excess inventory, and undelivered projects carry rising financing costs with revenue pushed out.
